newsitem.title: DUBAI: U.K. nurses' lawyer hails Australian court ruling.
newsitem.headline: U.K. nurses' lawyer hails Australian court ruling.

text.p: The lawyer for two British nurses charged with killing an Australian colleague in Saudi Arabia on Friday hailed a court ruling temporarily barring the victim's brother from demanding the death penalty.
"It is a great victory. The decision is honourable and just and we salute it...The threat of death penalty no longer exists," said Saudi lawyer Salah al-Hejailan.

"They don't have the death penalty in Australia and we have repeatedly asked Mr Guilford to be reasonable and cease from asking for the death penalty for our clients against whom there is no evidence," Hejailan told Reuters.

The South Australian state Supreme Court on Friday barred Frank Guilford, brother of the murder victim Yvonne Gilford, from calling for the death penalty for the two nurses and ordered him not to make further comments on behalf of his family until his mother's mental state had been assessed.
Under Saudi law, a call for the death penalty by a victim's family must be unanimous, lawyers representing the British nurses told the court.
The lawyers said Yvonne's mother, Muriel Gilford, suffers from Alzheimer's disease and is not mentally competent to agree with her son's call for execution.
Hejailan, speaking by telephone from the United States, said the information on Muriel Gilford's state of health was from "independent doctors and would stand up in further court inquiries".
Judge Len King issued a temporary restraining order against Frank Gilford pending a study of his mother's mental state.
King ordered Frank Gilford to notify the Saudi court of his ruling and that Muriel Gilford's health documents be made available to the British nurses' lawyers.

Yvonne Gilford, 51, was found murdered in her dormitory at the King Fahd medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dhahran on December 11 last year. She had been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.
British nurses Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLaughlan, 31, have been charged with murdering Gilford, but have said they are innocent, despite initially signing confessions.
If found guilty the nurses face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally a public beheading by the sword.

King said there was clear evidence Frank Gilford had told the Saudi court it was the unanimous view of the heirs that a death penalty should be imposed and that the consequences of a mistake in the matter could be dire and irreversible.
Dick Whitington, acting for Parry and McLaughlan, earlier told the court that there could be no execution if there was lack of unanimity among the heirs.
Whitington said Frank Gilford's statements representing his mother's view on the penalty were "knowingly false and malicious...(and) calculated to cause damage to (the British nurses)".
